claim: Tailwind v4's entry stylesheet is literally four lines: it declares the layer order `theme, base, components, utilities` and imports theme.css into `theme`, preflight.css into `base`, and utilities.css into `utilities`.

Per the CSS cascade spec, normal (non-!important) unlayered author styles always beat normal declarations inside any cascade layer, irrespective of specificity or source order; !important reverses this.
quote: Within author styles, all important declarations within CSS layers take precedence over any important declarations declared outside of a layer, while all normal declarations within CSS layers have a lower priority than declarations declared outside of a layer.

claim: Layer priority is declaration-order based: first-declared layer is lowest priority, last-declared is highest.
quote: The first declared layer gets the lowest priority and the last declared layer gets the highest priority. ... Styles that are not defined in a layer always override styles declared in named and anonymous layers.

claim: `@import url layer(layer-name)` assigns an entire third-party stylesheet into a named cascade layer, which is the mechanism for taming unlayered vendor CSS.
quote: The `layer` keyword or the `layer()` function is used with `@import` for this purpose. Declarations in style rules from imported stylesheets interact with the cascade as if they were written literally into the stylesheet at the point of the import.

claim: Tailwind v4 deliberately builds on native cascade layers and ships a first-party Vite plugin; benchmark full build 378ms (v3.4) -> 100ms (v4), incremental with new CSS 44ms -> 5ms, incremental with no new CSS 35ms -> 192 microseconds.
quote: Native cascade layers — giving us more control than ever over how different style rules interact with each other. ... we've found full rebuilds to be over 3.5x faster, and incremental builds to be over 8x faster. ... these builds are over 100x faster and complete in microseconds.

claim: A Tailwind collaborator confirms the root cause of Mantine (and any component-kit) styles beating Tailwind utilities in v4: utilities now live in a cascade layer and layers lose to unlayered rules. Documented workaround: import utilities.css WITHOUT layer() so utilities become unlayered.
quote: This is caused by the fact that Tailwind utility classes are now in cascade layers, which have lower precedence than rules not in any layer.

claim: Community discussion on Tailwind v4 vs third-party component libraries confirms unlayered CSS beats layered CSS regardless of specificity, and recommends `@import 'lib/styles.css' layer(thirdparty)` plus an explicit @layer order rather than specificity hacks.
quote: unlayered CSS beats layered CSS regardless of specificity. That's why it wins over your utilities ... Raises specificity: skip it. Fixes one collision, causes others. Layers are the built-in answer

claim: Preflight is Tailwind's opinionated reset injected into @layer base: it zeroes all margins/padding, sets box-sizing: border-box and border: 0 solid, unstyles headings (font-size/weight: inherit), removes list-style from ol/ul/menu, and makes img/svg/video/canvas/iframe display: block.
quote: *,::after,::before,::backdrop,::file-selector-button { margin: 0; padding: 0; } ... h1,h2,h3,h4,h5,h6 { font-size: inherit; font-weight: inherit; } ... ol,ul,menu { list-style: none; } ... img,svg,video,canvas,audio,iframe,embed,object { display: block; vertical-align: middle; }

claim: In Tailwind v4 you disable Preflight by expanding `@import "tailwindcss"` into its constituent imports and omitting the preflight.css import — there is no corePlugins toggle.

v4 breaking changes relevant to component kits: default border color changed gray-200 -> currentColor, placeholder color -> current text color at 50% opacity, button cursor -> default (was pointer); `corePlugins`, `safelist` and `separator` are unsupported in JS config; JS config must be loaded explicitly with `@config`.
quote: Unsupported options: corePlugins, safelist, separator ... Default Border Color: v3 used gray-200 by default; v4 changed to currentColor ... Button Cursor: v3 cursor: pointer by default; v4 cursor: default

claim: The important modifier moved from prefix (`!flex`) in v3 to suffix (`flex!`) in v4, and v3's `@layer utilities { .foo {} }` is replaced by the `@utility foo {}` directive.
quote: v3: <div class="!flex !bg-red-500"> ... v4: <div class="flex! bg-red-500!"> ... v3: @layer utilities { .tab-4 { tab-size: 4; } } ... v4: @utility tab-4 { tab-size: 4; }

claim: The `@utility` directive registers custom utilities into the built-in `utilities` layer (so they get variant support and correct sort order); `@layer base` and `@layer components` remain the way to add resets and overridable component classes.
quote: Custom utilities are automatically inserted into the `utilities` layer along with all of the built-in utilities in the framework.

claim: Tailwind v4 escape hatches for specificity: the `!` suffix on a single utility, and the `important` flag on the import which marks ALL utilities !important (which then also wins over unlayered third-party CSS).
quote: you can add `!` to the end of the class name to make all of the declarations `!important` ... If you're adding Tailwind to a project that has existing complex CSS with high specificity rules, you can use the `important` flag when importing Tailwind to mark all utilities as `!important`: @import "tailwindcss" important;

claim: Tailwind explicitly does NOT recommend combining CSS modules with Tailwind: each CSS module is processed separately by Vite/Parcel/Turbopack, so 50 modules means Tailwind runs 50 times, and modules have no @theme unless you add `@reference`.
quote: we don't recommend using CSS modules and Tailwind together if you can avoid it. ... if you have 50 CSS modules in a project, Tailwind needs to run 50 separate times, which leads to much slower build times and a worse developer experience. ... Since CSS modules are each processed separately, they have no @theme unless you import one.

claim: Tailwind v4 is itself a build tool (Lightning CSS based) and bundles @import natively, so postcss-import/Sass/Less/Stylus are unnecessary and unsupported.
quote: Tailwind CSS v4.0 is a full-featured CSS build tool designed for a specific workflow, and is not designed to be used with CSS preprocessors like Sass, Less, or Stylus. ... Tailwind will automatically bundle other CSS files you include with @import, without the need for a separate preprocessing tool.

claim: Vite auto-applies any valid postcss.config.* to ALL imported CSS, independent of Vite plugins; .module.css is handled as CSS modules; Lightning CSS can replace PostCSS only via experimental css.transformer.
quote: If the project contains valid PostCSS config (any format supported by postcss-load-config), it will be automatically applied to all imported CSS. ... Lightning CSS is used to minify CSS in production builds by default. However, PostCSS is still used for other CSS processing.

claim: @tailwindcss/vite is installed as a Vite plugin (`plugins: [tailwindcss()]`) with no postcss.config and no content globs; the alternative @tailwindcss/postcss path exists for frameworks that require PostCSS.

MUI's official Tailwind v4 integration requires opting Emotion output into a cascade layer via enableCssLayer and declaring `@layer theme, base, mui, components, utilities;` — otherwise Tailwind classes do not override MUI components.
quote:
<StyledEngineProvider enableCssLayer>
  <GlobalStyles styles="@layer theme, base, mui, components, utilities;" />
  {/* Your app */}
</StyledEngineProvider>

claim: enableCssLayer wraps all Material UI component and global styles in a single `@layer mui`; Next.js App Router uses AppRouterCacheProvider options={{ enableCssLayer: true }}.
quote: When enabled, Material UI uses `@layer mui` as the default single cascade layer for all components and global styles. ... <AppRouterCacheProvider options={{ enableCssLayer: true }}>

claim: Mantine ships parallel stylesheets wrapped in `@layer mantine` (styles.layer.css) precisely so Tailwind/other CSS can override it; you must not import both styles.css and styles.layer.css.
quote: All `@mantine/*` packages that export styles have an additional file in which all styles are wrapped in the `@layer mantine` directive. ... Do not import both `styles.css` and `styles.layer.css` ... If your styles are not wrapped in the `@layer` directive, they will be applied after Mantine styles

claim: Working Mantine + Tailwind v4 recipe: declare `@layer theme, base, mantine, components, utilities;` before importing tailwindcss and Mantine's layered stylesheet.
Measured Emotion runtime cost: a component rendering in 54.3ms with Emotion dropped to 27.7ms after removing it (~48% faster); runtime serialization recurs on every render.
quote: The Member Browser component rendered in 54.3ms with Emotion (on M1 Max), dropping to 27.7ms without it ... "This effectively causes a recalculation of all CSS rules against all DOM nodes every frame while React is rendering. This is VERY slow."

claim: React officially discourages runtime <style> tag injection (the Emotion/styled-components model): it forces frequent browser style recalculation and is unfixable; React recommends static CSS extraction plus inline styles instead.
quote: We don't recommend runtime <style> tag injection for two reasons: 1. Runtime injection forces the browser to recalculate the styles a lot more often. 2. Runtime injection can be very slow if it happens at the wrong time in the React lifecycle. The first problem is not solvable

claim: useInsertionEffect does not run on the server, so CSS-in-JS libraries need separate SSR collection paths — a structural friction point for RSC.
quote: Similarly to `useEffect`, `useInsertionEffect` does not run on the server. If you need to collect which CSS rules have been used on the server, you can do it during rendering
